Action Plan:
1) Acute wheeze/shortness of breath (suspected asthma flare):
- Increase salbutamol inhaler use to 2–4 puffs via spacer every 4 hours initially.
- Prescribe spacer; pharmacist to demonstrate correct use on collection.
- Prescribe peak flow meter; patient to measure and record peak flow twice daily (on waking and in the evening) for 1 week.
- Safety-net: Call back urgently if temperature becomes high or wheeze/shortness of breath worsens; seek urgent care if unable to speak in full sentences, symptoms at rest, chest pain, or cyanosis.
- Arrange GP/asthma review in approximately 1 week to review symptoms and peak flow diary; discuss need for additional controller medication based on response and readings.

2) Allergic rhinitis (hay fever) contributing to bronchospasm:
- Start a regular over-the-counter antihistamine (name/dose not documented); pharmacist can advise selection.

Verbal consent from patient has been obtained before using transcription software.

Subjective:
- Reason for visit: Wheeze and shortness of breath.
- History of present illness:
  - Onset: 2–3 days.
  - Symptoms: Wheeze, exertional dyspnea (cannot walk to work), occasional difficulty completing sentences during flare, dry cough.
  - Fever: Patient felt feverish; measured temperature 37°C.
  - Negatives: No chest pain, no sputum, no hemoptysis, no nocturnal awakening. Currently comfortable at rest; can climb stairs.
- Past medical history: Childhood asthma (“quite bad,” required inhalers; occasional hospital visits; no ICU). Atopy: hay fever and eczema.
- Medications: Salbutamol inhaler PRN (used every few weeks; also around exercise). No other routine meds.
- Allergies: No known drug allergies.
- Social history: Non-smoker. Alcohol ~1 glass of wine every 2–3 days. Lives with partner. Occupation: Engineer. Currently working from home/sick leave due to symptoms.

Objective:
- Telehealth consultation; no formal vitals or physical exam performed.
- Patient reports temperature 37°C.
- Functional status during call: Speaking comfortably at rest; able to manage stairs.

Investigations:
- None performed today.

Assessment & Plan:

1. Acute wheeze and exertional dyspnea:
   - Assessment / likely diagnosis: Asthma exacerbation (DDx: High likelihood).
   - Differential diagnosis (consistent with DDx):
     - Viral upper respiratory infection/acute bronchitis with bronchospasm (Medium): Short duration, dry cough; supports bronchospasm trigger. Opposes: afebrile, no upper respiratory symptoms reported.
     - COVID-19 infection precipitating asthma symptoms (Medium-Low): Cough/SOB possible. Opposes: normal temperature, no typical features/exposures noted.
     - Community-acquired pneumonia (Low): Cough/SOB, but afebrile, non-productive, well at rest.
     - Pulmonary embolism (Low): Acute dyspnea possible; opposes: no pleuritic chest pain/hemoptysis/risk factors; presence of wheeze; comfortable at rest.
   - Investigations planned: Peak flow monitoring twice daily for 1 week using prescribed peak flow meter.
   - Treatment planned:
     - Salbutamol inhaler 2–4 puffs via spacer every 4 hours initially.
     - Spacer prescribed; pharmacist to teach technique.
     - Safety-net advice as above; call back if fever develops or wheeze worsens.
   - Relevant referrals/follow-up: GP/asthma review in ~1 week to assess control and peak flow diary; consider need for additional controller inhaler based on response.

2. Allergic rhinitis (hay fever):
   - Assessment / likely diagnosis: Allergic rhinitis.
   - Differential diagnosis: Not discussed.
   - Investigations planned: None today.
   - Treatment planned: Begin regular over-the-counter antihistamine (specific agent/dose not documented).
   - Relevant referrals: None today.

Quality checks:
- Missing/expected elements:
  - No formal vitals (HR, RR, SpO2, BP) obtained due to telehealth.
  - No baseline or predicted peak flow recorded yet.
  - Inhaler technique not demonstrated during call; to be reviewed by pharmacist.
  - Specific antihistamine name/dose not documented.
  - Full medication reconciliation beyond salbutamol not performed.
- Conflicts between transcript and DDx: Patient reported “fever,” but measured temperature was 37°C; DDx lists viral/COVID possibilities noting afebrile status (no conflict; clarification noted).
- Transcript quality: Generally adequate; some responses unclear due to communication barriers; no in-person exam.
